title: Expense receipts and reports for consultants on Mac: how to match each receipt

description: Match each receipt to its card charge and expense report line on Mac. Costs, causes, a weekly routine and fixes you can use without buying software.

intro: Matching receipts to expense report lines means pairing each card charge with one receipt and a short business reason. Do it every week, not at month end, and you catch problems while the details are still fresh. This page covers what the mess costs, why it happens, and fixes you can use on a Mac today without buying anything.
tldr: Match every card charge to one receipt, checking amount, merchant, date and card.
Scan paper receipts the same day with Preview or Continuity Camera on your Mac.
Keep an Excel log with a Status column, and filter on Missing before you submit.
Watch same-vendor charges on adjacent days and pending charges. They cause wrong matches.
Lazur can point, explain, guide and draft. It does not match receipts or change files for you.

blocks.text: A match is a small decision, repeated for every charge on your card. Each receipt should point to one card line. Each card line should point to one receipt, or to a written reason why there is none. Skip that check and the report looks finished. The mistakes show up later, when someone in finance sends it back.
How a receipt matches a card charge

Most matching logic checks the same few facts. Ramp documents its rules in its help center. It compares the amount, the merchant, the transaction date and the card details. It treats a receipt dated within one calendar day of the charge as a date match. You can run the same four checks by hand in a sheet.

rows: The receipt total equals the card charge
Tips added later, currency conversion and partial refunds change the total
The vendor name on the receipt matches the card line
Card lines can show a payment processor name instead of the store
The receipt falls within one calendar day of the charge
Hotels and trains can post days after the stay or trip
The receipt belongs to the card that paid
Personal and client cards get mixed into one log
blocks.caption: Four checks to run on every line, based on Ramp's documented rules.

blocks.text: Pending charges need extra care. A charge can show as pending before it posts, and its amount can change when it does. Ramp can match receipts to pending charges, but a match made too early may need a redo. Mark those lines Pending and come back to them after they post.
Where wrong matches come from

The classic wrong match is a repeat charge. Two dinners at the same restaurant, on adjacent days, with the same total, look identical to a date and amount check. Ramp warns about this exact pattern. Its fix is to attach the receipt by hand, then move it to the correct charge if it landed on the wrong one.

Consultant work adds a twist. You may stay at the same hotel for several client projects in a row. The vendor, the rate and the dates can all look alike. Read the guest name, the check-in date and the project code on the receipt before you trust a match.
Set up an expense receipts sheet in Excel on Mac
You do not need new software for this. One Excel workbook covers a trip or a month. Use one row per card charge, and keep the receipt file name in that row. That way you can find any file quickly.

items: Open a blank workbook in Excel. In row 1, type these headings: Date, Merchant, Amount, Client code, Receipt file, Status.
Copy each card line from your statement into the rows below the headings. Use the transaction date for the Date column.
Select the whole range, then choose Insert > Table. Excel adds banded rows and filter buttons.
Save the workbook in one folder you can find fast. Press ⌘S after each session.
When you check for a duplicate, press ⌘F and search the merchant name.

blocks.text: Add a Status column with three values: Matched, Missing and Pending. Select the header row and choose Data > Filter. Then filter on Missing before each send. That one filter shows you what is left, so you never send a report with blank lines.
Scan paper receipts on your Mac

Paper is the slowest part of the job. Apple gives you two built-in routes. With a scanner, open Preview and choose File > Import from Scanner > [scanner name]. Pick Document Feeder for a stack of receipts, or Flatbed for a single one. Set Orientation to Duplex if both sides matter.

Without a scanner, use your iPhone. Continuity Camera needs macOS Mojave 10.14 or later and iOS 12 or later. Turn on Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on both devices. Sign in with the same Apple Account, with two-factor authentication on. Then open Mail or Notes, Control-click where the scan should go, and choose Insert from iPhone or iPad > Scan Documents.

Preview has an iPhone route too. Choose File > Import from iPhone or iPad > Scan Documents. Either way, scan each receipt, name it, and drop it in your folder before you pick up the next one. A pile of unnamed scans is the start of a bad week.
Pull receipts out of your email

Many receipts never touch paper. They arrive as order confirmations and PDF invoices. Search your inbox each week for the word receipt, the word invoice and the vendor names you use most. Save each PDF into the same folder as your scans. For mail setup, see [Outlook for consultants on Mac](/for/consultants/outlook).

Keep one naming rule for every file. Use the date, the merchant and the amount, in that order. Dates first keep the folder in time order when you sort by name. A rule you follow every time beats a clever one you forget.
Some receipts exist only on screen, such as a booking page. Press ⌘⇧4, drag over the part you need, and save the screenshot to your folder. Then name it like any other receipt.
Mistakes that force a second pass

items: Matching from memory at month end, when the trip details have faded.
Trusting the total alone. Two different charges can share one amount.
Mixing personal and client charges on one card line without a note.
Leaving receipts as unnamed phone photos, then hunting for them later.
Leaving pending charges unmarked, so they look matched when they are not.

blocks.text: Each mistake sends the report back to you. Fixing one row often means reopening the month. Check the sheet weekly, so you fix a single row instead of a whole stack.
Handle missing receipts in an expense report

Some receipts are gone for good. Rho's 2024 survey lists lost receipts among the top three pain points for expense reports. Do not invent a receipt. Mark the row Missing, and ask the vendor for a copy if they offer one.

Then follow your employer's rule for missing receipts. Some companies accept a signed statement with the date, vendor, amount and business reason. Others will not pay without a receipt. Ask finance which rule applies before you write one.
Client data and confidentiality

Receipts often show client names, project codes and travel plans. Treat them as client material. Check your firm's and your client's rules before you share a receipt with a scanner app, an outside tool or an AI assistant. If your employer sets a policy, follow it first.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those facts do not replace your employer's rules.
Where the time goes in expense reports

GBTA's study ranks the biggest pain points. Attaching receipts came first at 37%. Entering data came next at 33%, and setting up the report came third at 24%. Receipts are the largest single step, so this page starts there.

Read those percentages as direction, not precision. The study was sponsored by HRS Global Hotel Solutions, and its page gives no sample size or method. Use it to decide where to spend your effort, not to forecast your own hours.
When a tool helps and when a sheet is enough

Software with built-in matching saves time once the volume grows. Ramp documents matching on amount, merchant and date, plus pending charges. That only helps if your firm uses the card and the tool. Rho reports that only 29% of workers have access to corporate card expense management software.

For a few trips a month, a sheet, a scanner and a weekly filter are enough. Lazur is not a matching tool. It does not attach files or change cells for you. It can point, explain, guide you through steps and draft the note to finance.
Check the total before you submit

Before you submit, run three checks. Every card line should show Matched, or a written reason. Every receipt file should appear in the sheet once. The matched total should equal the card total for the same period on your statement. Pending lines must clear first.
If the totals differ, check for two causes first. A missed receipt leaves a gap. A duplicate receipt adds one. Find the gap in the sheet, then go back to the email or the paper pile.
Where Lazur fits in this routine

faq.answer: No. Lazur does not read your bank feed, attach files or change cells for you. It can explain what is on screen, point at the column you need, guide you through each click and draft a note. You make the match.

faq.question: What if I lost a receipt?
faq.answer: Mark the row Missing. Ask the vendor for a copy if they offer one. Then follow your employer's missing receipt rule. Do not write a receipt yourself.

faq.question: Is it safe to show client receipts to Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Still, follow your firm's and your client's rules first.

faq.question: Do I need expense software to do this?
faq.answer: No. A workbook, a scanner or your iPhone, and a weekly slot cover a small volume. Software helps as volume grows, and when your firm supplies it. Rho reports that only 29% of workers have access to corporate card expense management software.

faq.question: Why did a receipt attach to the wrong charge?
faq.answer: Same-vendor charges on adjacent days, with the same amount, are the usual cause. Ramp advises attaching the receipt manually, then re-attaching it to the correct charge if it was misfiled.

costs.title: Time on every report
costs.text: Rho's 2024 survey found about 75% of employees take over 15 minutes per report. Webexpenses' older 2017 survey put the average at 41 minutes a month. Both are vendor surveys, so treat them as direction, not a precise budget.

costs.title: Corrections cost more than first passes
costs.text: GBTA reports that 19% of expense reports contain errors or missing information. Its article puts each correction at $52 and 18 minutes. A 2015 GBTA press release gives $58 and 18 minutes, so the dollar figure is uncertain. The time figure matches in both.

costs.title: The company-level bill
costs.text: GBTA says companies process an average of 51,000 expense reports each year. It estimates they spend about half a million dollars and nearly 3,000 hours correcting errors annually. Those are company totals, not one consultant's bill.

costs.title: Billable time you never bill
costs.text: Consultants bill by the hour, so every hour spent on receipts is an hour away from client work. No study found measured this for consultants. Time one month of matching, then value those hours at your own rate.

costs.title: Reimbursement delay
costs.text: A rejected line can hold up the whole report. You may wait for a second pass before you are repaid. Your firm's policy sets how long that takes, so ask finance instead of guessing.

causes.title: Receipts come from too many places
causes.text: Paper receipts go in pockets. Phone photos stay in the camera roll. Vendor emails sit in an inbox. Each source needs its own step, and each step is a chance to lose a receipt. GBTA found attaching receipts was the top pain point in its study.

causes.title: Card lines do not look like receipts
causes.text: A card line shows a processor name, a posting date and a total that can change after a tip. A receipt shows the store name and the time of sale. The two often differ in name, date or total, so each match takes judgment.

causes.title: Matching waits until month end
causes.text: Memory fades over a month. Details that seemed obvious on the day, like which client a dinner was for, turn into guesses. Rho reports that about 60% of employees file daily or weekly, which shows how much a regular habit matters.

causes.title: Data entry and setup eat the time
causes.text: The GBTA study ranks entering data (33%) and setting up the report (24%) as pain points, right after receipts. Every line you retype is another chance for a typo. A sheet that mirrors the card statement cuts the retyping.

causes.title: No system at all
causes.text: Rho found only 29% of workers have access to corporate card expense management software. Without that software, matching falls to you, a spreadsheet and your memory. People often build a system only after a missed receipt costs them time.

causes.title: Repeat charges look alike
causes.text: Repeat charges from one vendor, with the same total and close dates, make wrong matches likely. Ramp documents this as a known failure mode for automatic matching, and it applies to hand matching too.

fixes.title: Scan or photograph on the same day
fixes.text: Use Preview or Continuity Camera as soon as a receipt lands in your hand. Set Document Feeder for a stack. A same-day scan takes far less effort than the search you run a month later.

fixes.title: Name every file the same way
fixes.text: Use date, merchant and amount, in that order. Dates first keep the folder sorted by time. Consistent names let you match the folder and the sheet in one pass.

fixes.title: Filter the sheet on Missing
fixes.text: Mark each row Matched, Missing or Pending. Select the header row and choose Data > Filter in Excel. Before you send anything, work the Missing list until it is empty or each row has a written reason.

fixes.title: Check the neighbors of every repeat
fixes.text: Match on amount, merchant and date first. Then look at the same vendor one day before and one day after. If two charges look alike, attach the receipt by hand and confirm the correct line before you move on.

fixes.title: Hold pending charges until they post
fixes.text: Mark pending lines as Pending and leave them alone. A charge can change when it posts, so a match made too early may need a redo. Revisit those rows at your weekly session.

fixes.title: Schedule one weekly session
fixes.text: Pick one fixed time each week, such as a Friday afternoon. Add it to Apple Reminders so it happens. Rho reports that about 60% of employees file daily or weekly, so a regular slot is common practice.

fixes.title: Capture screen-only receipts with a screenshot
fixes.text: Some receipts exist only as a booking page. Press ⌘⇧4, drag over the part you need, and save the file to your receipts folder. Name it like any other receipt so it can match the card line.

fixes.title: Check totals before you submit
fixes.text: Add up the matched amounts for the period. Compare that total with the card statement for the same period. Any gap points to a missing receipt, or to a receipt attached twice.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Build the sheet
plan.text: Create one Excel workbook with Date, Merchant, Amount, Client code, Receipt file and Status columns. Choose Insert > Table and save the file in a folder you know. Enter every card line for the period first, so each row exists before you hunt for receipts.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Scan paper receipts
plan.text: Scan everything in your wallet and bag. Use Document Feeder if you have a scanner, or Continuity Camera if you use your iPhone. Name each file the same way and save it in one folder.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Pull email receipts
plan.text: Search Outlook for receipt, invoice and each vendor name. Save the PDFs into the same folder as your scans. Add each file to the sheet as you go, so nothing sits unlogged.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Match and mark
plan.text: Match each card line to one file, then mark it Matched, Missing or Pending. Check the same vendor on the days before and after. Attach by hand whenever two charges look alike.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Chase and check
plan.text: Filter the sheet on Missing. Ask vendors for copies, or follow your employer's rule for missing receipts. Add up the matched amounts and compare them with the card statement before you submit.

plan.label: Every Friday
plan.title: Repeat the short session
plan.text: Run the email search and the matching again, but only for the new charges. Keep the sheet open all week, so receipts never pile up into a month-end job.
